title: First-in-Order Pick of Every Letter
statement:
You get a string s of lowercase letters. Pick a subsequence of s (delete some characters, keep the order of the rest) that contains every distinct letter of s exactly once.

Among all such subsequences, return the one that comes first in dictionary order.

examples.why: Starting with a works, but then the only b left is the very last letter, so "ab…" is impossible. The best continuation is c, d, then that final b. Sorting the letters ("abcd") is not a valid pick.
The only a is at index 3 and no c comes after it, so c has to come before a. Starting with b still leaves the c at index 2 and the a at index 3.
x can lead because z and y both appear again later. Then z, then y, each from the second half.

constraints: s has only lowercase English letters
hints: Build the answer left to right. When a new letter is smaller than the last letter you kept, when is it safe to throw that last letter away?
You may drop the last kept letter only if it appears again later in s, so you can pick it up again. Precompute the last index of each letter.
Keep the answer in a stack. Skip letters already in it. Otherwise pop while the top is bigger than the current letter and occurs again later, then push the current letter.

explain.intuition:
Dictionary order is decided by the earliest position that differs, so you want small letters as early as possible. When you are holding ...d and see a c, the answer would be better with c before d. You can only make that swap if there is another d later to pick up instead. So: pop a bigger letter when it is "replaceable", keep it when it is the last copy.

A stack does exactly this, like the undo stack in an editor: the most recent choice is the first you reconsider. Each letter is pushed and popped at most once, so it is linear.
steps: Record last[c], the last index of each letter in s.
Walk s with index i. If s[i] is already in the stack, skip it.
While the stack's top is greater than s[i] and last[top] > i, pop it and mark it as not in the stack.
Push s[i] and mark it as in the stack.
Join the stack into the answer.
pitfalls: Not skipping letters already in the stack. They would be pushed twice, or would pop letters that a better earlier copy already placed.
Popping a letter whose last copy has already passed. It can never be picked again, so the answer would miss it.
Returning the distinct letters sorted. The first example shows that order may be impossible.

complexity.space: O(1) (at most 26 letters on the stack)

solutions.title: Try every subsequence
solutions.idea: Enumerate all subsequences, keep those with each distinct letter exactly once, and take the smallest.

solutions.title: Pick the smallest safe letter, repeatedly
solutions.idea: The next answer letter is the smallest letter c such that everything still needed appears at or after c's first occurrence in the remaining text. Take it, cut s just after it, and remove c everywhere.

solutions.title: Monotonic stack
solutions.idea: Keep the answer on a stack. Pop bigger letters that appear again later, then push the current letter if it is not already used.

followups: Return the subsequence that comes last in dictionary order instead.
Each distinct letter must appear exactly twice in the result. How does the stack rule change?
